read: partial: main text pp.1-9 (abstract, introduction, related work, data creation and expert review, ChainEval, experiments, error analysis, conclusion, limitations, ethics, acknowledgements) in full; appendices A.1, A.3-A.4, B.1-B.6 and D.1-D.5 (pp.13-22) read; A.2 (template code), C, E and F skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2506.02515v4, 30 Apr 2026 (p.1); no venue in the text, which thanks anonymous reviewers (p.9)
what_it_is: FinChain is a symbolic benchmark for verifiable chain-of-thought financial reasoning. It has 290 parameterised templates (two basic, two intermediate and one advanced per topic) over 58 topics in 12 financial domains, written as executable Python programs that generate each question together with its intermediate steps and final answer (pp.2-4, 13). The templates were written with LLM assistance, following GSM-Symbolic, and curated by financial experts: ten experts calibrated on 20 templates, then one expert reviewed each of the other 270, and 29 of the 290 were found incorrect and revised (pp.3-4, 15). The test set has 10 instances per template, 2,900 in all (p.6). Its ChainEval metric aligns a model's steps with the gold steps by dynamic time warping, crediting a pair only when their sentence embeddings are similar and their intermediate results agree within 5%, and adds final-answer correctness with weight 0.1 (pp.4-5). Twenty-six LLMs were evaluated zero-shot (p.5).
domain: finance: 12 domains and 58 topics, e.g. corporate finance, financial reporting, risk management, crypto finance (p.3)
size: 290 templates (116 basic, 116 intermediate, 58 advanced, with mean gold chains of 2.01, 2.97 and 3.90 steps) (p.4); 2,900 test instances (p.6); 26 LLMs (p.5)
source_of_items: generated from templates; the templates were LLM-drafted and expert-curated (pp.3-4, 13)
has_gold_traces: yes: each template's executable Python solution yields a gold chain of steps with an intermediate result per step (pp.2-4)
evaluation: step-level, reference-based: ChainEval = 0.9 x a DTW alignment score over gold and predicted steps (the cosine similarity of sentence embeddings x an indicator that the step results agree within 5% relative) + 0.1 x final-answer correctness at 5% tolerance (pp.4-5). Steps are extracted by regular expressions, with GPT-4.1 splitting steps when no 'Step x' pattern is found and extracting the final answer (pp.7, 21-22). ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L and BERTScore are reported for comparison (p.7).
human_validation: Templates: ten financial experts (seven graduate students, three industry professionals); a 20-template pilot reviewed by all, after which all agreed; the remaining 270 reviewed by one expert each; 29 of 290 (10%) found incorrect and revised (pp.15, 17). Metric: 100 responses (20 instances x 5 models) rated 1-5 by financial experts for reasoning-process quality and final-answer accuracy (pp.5-6); the Spearman correlation with the process ratings is 0.655 for ChainEval, against 0.469 for ROUGE-2, 0.434 for ROUGE-L and 0.287 for BERTScore (Table 5, p.20). No inter-rater agreement is reported. The error-analysis labels on 200 questions are expert-validated (p.8).
contamination_measures: generated instances: the templates are said to allow 'contamination-free' generation (pp.1, 9), but no contamination test is reported, and the templates and code are public under the MIT licence (p.9)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-I2 (L84-94, Introduction): 'Symbolic templates (Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025) serve as the generative mechanism, producing unique, contamination-resistant instances'
engtrace_use.explanation: The narrow claim is accurate. FinChain's parameterised symbolic templates, which follow Mirzadeh et al., generate the instances and are described as enabling scalable, contamination-free generation (pp.1-3). Its 10 instances per template come from distinct random seeds (p.6), though uniqueness is not checked. But the sentence omits what matters most for the comparison. FinChain already pairs every generated instance with an executable gold chain of thought and scores step-level alignment with it (pp.2, 4-5). The May paper presents exactly this as its own contribution in the sentence before: 'a symbolic benchmark pairing each problem instance with a gold-standard reasoning trace to enable verifiable process supervision' (L81-84). Related Work never discusses FinChain. The claim at L77-80 that no existing benchmark verifies this process is scoped to engineering, so it is not false, but citing FinChain only for its templates hides that the template-plus-gold-trace design and step-level scoring are FinChain's. The verdict is misleading under the protocol's 'omits what matters most for the comparison'; the words of S-I2 themselves are accurate.

suggested_wording: Closest to EngTrace is FinChain (Xie et al., 2025), whose parameterised financial templates generate each instance together with an executable gold chain of thought, and whose ChainEval metric aligns a model's steps with the gold steps, crediting a pair only when their wording is similar and their intermediate results agree within 5%, alongside final-answer correctness.
facts_to_cite: Symbolic templates following Mirzadeh et al., written as executable Python programs that generate the question, the intermediate steps and the final answer (pp.2-3; Fig. 1, p.1)

12 financial domains, 58 topics and five templates per topic (two basic, two intermediate, one advanced), 290 templates in all, with mean gold chains of 2.01, 2.97 and 3.90 steps by tier (pp.2-4; Table 1, p.4)
10 instances per template give 2,900 test instances (p.6)

The templates were LLM-drafted and expert-curated; after a 20-template calibration pilot, each of the other 270 was reviewed by one of ten financial experts, and 29 of 290 were found incorrect and revised (pp.4, 15, 17)

ChainEval aligns gold and predicted steps by dynamic time warping, crediting a step pair only when their embedding similarity is high and their results agree within 5%, and combines this with final-answer correctness at weight 0.1 (pp.4-5)
Validated on 100 responses rated by financial experts: Spearman 0.655 with process-quality ratings, against 0.469 for ROUGE-2 and 0.287 for BERTScore (pp.5-6; Table 5, p.20)
26 LLMs evaluated, spanning frontier, finance-specific, math-enhanced and general open-weight models; frontier models lead but degrade on advanced templates (pp.5-8)
The paper notes that correct final answers do not necessarily imply faithful intermediate reasoning (p.7)
Its stated limitations: the data are entirely synthetic and may lack linguistic diversity, and scoring depends on parsing the model's chain of thought (p.9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares almost the whole design: generated instances from parameterised symbolic templates; an executable gold trace per instance; step-level evaluation against that trace plus final-answer correctness; expert review of templates; expert validation of the metric; difficulty tiers; a roster spanning frontier, domain-tuned and math-enhanced models. Where it differs or falls short: the domain (finance, not engineering); depth (gold chains of 2 to 4 steps on average, p.4, and a single target per template, p.15, while EngTrace also has multipart, vector, array, symbolic and classification answers); tolerance (5% at every step and for the answer, p.5, against EngTrace's 0.002 relative answer tolerance and 0.5% milestones); the checker (embedding similarity gated by value agreement, validated by one rank correlation on 100 responses with no inter-rater agreement, against EngTrace's deterministic value checks and residual judge, validated against 15 experts with Fleiss kappa, AUROC and planted defects); template certification (one expert per template after calibration, against three own-branch experts per template with planted defects); contamination (public, MIT-licensed templates and no test, against EngTrace's private seed, hashed pool and paraphrase test). These differences, not the change of domain alone, are what EngTrace must say it adds.
notes: Authorship: four EngTrace authors are FinChain authors (Zhuohan Xie, Fan Zhang, Veselin Stoyanov, Preslav Nakov; FinChain p.1, May paper p.1). FinChain also lists Rania Elbadry (MBZUAI) and EngTrace lists Rania Hossam (MBZUAI); whether they are the same person cannot be told from the texts. FinChain's acknowledgements thank EngTrace's first two authors, Muhammad Usman Safder and Ayesha Gull, as student volunteers who built its live demo and website (p.9). The revised text must still cite FinChain in the third person, for ARR anonymity. Several May-paper elements mirror FinChain: Figure 1's template, variables and chain-of-thought layout (FinChain Fig. 1, p.1), the comparison of a process metric with ROUGE-2 and BERTScore (FinChain pp.6-7, 20), and a roster split into frontier, open-weight and math-enhanced models (p.5). A reviewer who knows FinChain will read the May design as FinChain moved to engineering unless the differences above are stated. The May reference entry has no identifier (citation map C15a); the arXiv id is 2506.02515, and its 25 authors match the paper (p.1). EngTrace should not echo FinChain's 'contamination-free', which FinChain does not test.
